turns.reply:
Hi! Today we're looking at components that change how they work depending on their surroundings — and how some stay steady no matter what. Let's start with the simplest: a fixed resistor, which keeps the same resistance when temperature stays constant.

What shape do you get when you plot current against potential difference for a fixed resistor?

Right — it is a straight line! That straight line tells us something important: when you push twice as much voltage through a fixed resistor, you get twice as much current. The resistance stays the same, doing its job steadily.

What do we call a resistor that keeps the same resistance like this?
It's called an ohmic conductor. Now, some resistors aren't fixed — you can actually change their resistance by hand using a sliding contact. What might you use one for?

turns.student: like controlling volume on a speaker?
turns.reply: Yes — volume control is a perfect example! So when you slide that contact along, what are you actually changing about the resistor?

turns.student: the resistance like goes up or down?
turns.reply: Exactly — the resistance goes up or down as you move that contact. Now, here's something different. Some components don't just have fixed or changeable resistance — some components only let current flow in *one direction*. A diode is like a one-way gate for electricity. What do you think that one-way property might be useful for?
recap: A fixed resistor keeps the same resistance, and current and voltage have a straight-line relationship.
Ohmic conductors follow this pattern — double the voltage and you double the current.
Variable resistors have a sliding contact that lets you change the resistance up or down.
You can use variable resistors for practical things like controlling speaker volume.

turns.reply:
I get it — let me make it simpler. Think of a diode like a one-way valve: it lets water flow one way easily, but blocks it the other way almost completely.

What happens to the resistance when you try to push current backwards through a diode?

Right — very high resistance in the reverse direction, so only a tiny bit of current can squeeze through. Now, a diode that gives out light when current flows forwards is called an LED, or light-emitting diode. You'll find LEDs everywhere — in phone screens, traffic lights, and energy-efficient light bulbs. Where have you spotted an LED recently?

LEDs are really handy — they're bright, use very little power, and last ages, which is why your phone and TV use them instead of old light bulbs. You probably see them flashing or glowing all the time without even noticing.

What colour LED have you got on a device near you right now?
Would you like me to just run through the rest of the diode stuff quickly?

Cool, we're doing well then. So an LED is just a diode that gives out light when current flows through it the right way — that's the forward direction. You'll find them in phone screens, traffic lights, and loads of other devices.

What's one thing you like about LEDs compared to old light bulbs?

turns.student: idk tbh they just work innit
turns.reply:
Fair enough! So the thing is, LEDs only work when current goes through them the right way — the forward direction. If you try to connect them backwards, basically nothing happens because the diode blocks it.

What would happen if you put an LED into a circuit but connected it backwards?

So an LED is a diode that gives out light when current flows through it the right way. Its resistance changes depending on how bright or dark it is around it. The brighter the light, the lower its resistance gets. What happens to an LDR's resistance when it gets darker?
recap: A diode is a one-way gate that lets current flow easily in one direction but blocks it the other way.
LEDs are light-emitting diodes — they glow when current flows through them in the forward direction only.
If you connect an LED backwards, the high resistance means no current flows and it won't light up.
LEDs are used everywhere because they're bright, use very little power, and last a really long time.

turns.reply:
Actually, let me flip that around — when it gets darker, there's *less* light, so the LDR's resistance goes *up*, not down. It's the opposite way round.

So in bright sunlight, the LDR's resistance gets really low — maybe just a few hundred ohms. What happens to that resistance when you cover it up and it gets dark?

Fair enough — grab a snack if you need to!

So there's another component called a thermistor, and it's a bit like the LDR but it responds to *temperature* instead of light. The hotter it gets, the lower its resistance drops.

What do you reckon happens to a thermistor's resistance when the temperature gets really cold?
recap: An LDR's resistance drops when it's bright and increases when it's dark.
In strong sunlight, an LDR can have a resistance of just a few hundred ohms.
The relationship works the opposite way to what you might first guess.

turns.reply:
A thermistor just responds to heat — when it's cold, its resistance is high, and when it's hot, its resistance drops down low.

What happens to the thermistor's resistance when temperature goes down?

Right — when it gets cold, the thermistor's resistance goes up, just like you said.

You've now covered all the big ideas: diodes, LDRs, thermistors, and how they change with light and heat. That's the whole lesson done!
recap: A thermistor is a component that changes resistance based on temperature.
When it gets hot, the resistance decreases.
When it gets cold, the resistance increases.

turns.reply: No problem at all — you've done really well today covering diodes, LDRs, and thermistors. Come back anytime you want to go over it again or move on to something new. Good luck with your revision!
